body:
The emergence of modern Indian painting

Modern Indian painting developed during the colonial period, particularly from the 19th century onwards. It did not replace India's older painting traditions in a single movement. Instead, Indian painters began working with new materials, methods, institutions and ideas while continuing to draw inspiration from Indian society, literature and cultural heritage.

Two important developments shaped this period. The first was the growing influence of European academic realism, which encouraged painters to represent people and objects with lifelike proportions, light, shadow and depth. The second was the search for an artistic style that expressed an independent Indian cultural identity. This search became particularly important during the growth of Indian nationalism.

European academic realism

During British rule, art schools introduced systematic training in European methods of drawing and painting. Artists increasingly used oil paints, canvas, perspective and studies of the human figure. These methods helped painters create convincing portraits and scenes that appeared three-dimensional.

Academic realism is a style of painting that attempts to represent visible subjects realistically through accurate proportions, modelling of forms, perspective and the effects of light and shadow.

The use of European techniques did not necessarily mean that the subjects were European. An Indian painter could use oil paints and realistic modelling to depict an episode from the Ramayana or Mahabharata. Raja Ravi Varma became a leading example of this combination.

The search for an Indian artistic identity

By the beginning of the 20th century, some artists argued that Indian painting should develop not only Indian subjects but also an artistic language inspired by India's own traditions. They turned towards historical paintings, particularly Mughal and Pahari miniatures, and experimented with softer colours and expressive compositions.

Abanindranath Tagore became the central figure of this movement, which came to be known as the Bengal School of Art. Its development was associated with the cultural nationalism and Swadeshi ideas of the period.

Why these developments must be distinguished

Modern Indian painting was not a single uniform style. Raja Ravi Varma and the Bengal School both used Indian cultural subjects, but their artistic approaches differed. Ravi Varma gave Indian stories a realistic appearance through European-influenced oil painting. Bengal School artists sought an alternative to European academic realism by drawing more directly on Indian painting traditions.

Regional painters, including artists from Gujarat, also participated in the development of modern Indian art. Their contributions included individual paintings, art education, publications and the establishment of institutions that encouraged new generations of artists.

The distinction is between subject matter and painting style. An Indian subject does not automatically mean that a painting follows a traditional Indian style.

Prelims focus

  • Modern Indian painting expanded during the 19th and early 20th centuries.
  • European academic realism emphasised lifelike representation, perspective, light and shadow.
  • Raja Ravi Varma combined Indian subjects with European-influenced realistic painting.
  • Abanindranath Tagore was the central figure of the Bengal School of Art.
  • The Bengal School drew inspiration from Indian painting traditions, including Mughal and Pahari miniatures.
  • Trap: Raja Ravi Varma and Abanindranath Tagore should not be assigned the same artistic approach merely because both painted Indian subjects.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, An Introduction to Indian Art—Part II, Chapter 6, The Bengal School and Cultural Nationalism, pp. 85–90, reprint 2025–26; National Gallery of Modern Art, Raja Ravi Varma: Artist's Profile, accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Modern Indian painting developed through encounters between Indian traditions and European artistic methods.

title: Modern Indian Painting: Colonial Influence and the Search for an Indian Style

body:
Life and artistic importance

Raja Ravi Varma (1848–1906) was one of the most prominent Indian painters of the 19th century. He was born at Kilimanoor in Travancore, in present-day Kerala.

He is especially remembered for combining European-influenced realistic painting with subjects drawn from Indian literature, mythology and everyday life. He also became an accomplished portrait painter, receiving commissions from members of royal families and other patrons.

Realistic representation of Indian subjects

Ravi Varma used oil paints to create convincing human figures. His paintings employed light and shadow to give bodies and objects a sense of volume. Attention to facial expressions, clothing and physical surroundings made the scenes appear immediate and lifelike.

His subjects frequently came from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and other Indian literary and religious traditions. He also painted portraits of prominent individuals and representations of Indian women.

Paintings associated with Ravi Varma include depictions of Shakuntala and Saraswati. His use of recognisable Indian subjects helped audiences relate to the paintings even though their visual treatment was strongly influenced by European academic methods.

Portrait painting and royal commissions

Portraiture was an important part of Ravi Varma's career. A portrait attempts to represent a particular person, rather than a general character or an imagined figure. Royal patrons valued portraits because they preserved the appearance of rulers and members of their families and could be displayed in palaces and public collections.

Ravi Varma travelled to fulfil commissions from princely courts. The Gaekwad court of Baroda was among his important patrons. This connection is particularly significant when studying the development of modern painting in Gujarat.

How printed reproductions expanded his influence

An original oil painting is a unique artwork. It may be displayed in a palace, museum or private collection, but its physical location limits the number of people who can see it directly. Ravi Varma recognised that printed reproductions could reach a much wider audience.

He established a lithographic printing enterprise in the Bombay region in 1894. The press produced inexpensive reproductions of paintings, including oleographs. These prints brought images based on his work into homes and other everyday settings.

Lithography is a method of printing images from a prepared printing surface. An oleograph is a colour print, commonly made using a lithographic process, that can reproduce the appearance of an oil painting.

The spread of such images was significant because it changed how art reached the public. A painting commissioned by a wealthy patron could become familiar to people who had never visited a royal court or art gallery. Printed images also helped popularise particular visual representations of Indian literary and religious figures.

Original paintings and printed images

Ravi Varma's reputation rests on both his original paintings and the wide circulation of images through printing. The two should not be confused: an oleograph is a printed reproduction, not an original oil painting made by the artist's hand. Moreover, some printed editions of his images continued to be produced after his death.

Prelims focus

  • Raja Ravi Varma lived from 1848 to 1906.
  • His birthplace was Kilimanoor in present-day Kerala.
  • He is associated with realistic oil painting, portraits and Indian mythological subjects.
  • His paintings drew subjects from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
  • His printing enterprise began in the Bombay region in 1894.
  • Trap: Oleographs helped circulate his images, but an oleograph is a print rather than an original oil painting.

[Sources: National Gallery of Modern Art, Raja Ravi Varma: Artist's Profile and collection descriptions of oil paintings and oleographs, accessed 23 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, An Introduction to Indian Art—Part II, Chapter 6, pp. 86–87, reprint 2025–26; GSEB Solutions, Class 8 Social Science, Chapter 7, Art in Modern India, questions concerning Ravi Varma and the printing press, accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Raja Ravi Varma’s unique oil painting leads through his 1894 Bombay-region printing enterprise to colour oleographs in households and popular visual culture.
pictures.caption: Printing enabled images based on a single painting to reach many viewers.

title: Raja Ravi Varma: Realistic Painting, Indian Themes and Popular Prints

body:
Baroda as a centre of artistic patronage

During the 19th century, Indian princely states continued to play an important role in supporting artists. Rulers commissioned portraits, historical scenes and paintings based on Indian literary traditions. Such commissions provided artists with income, recognition and opportunities to produce large works.

Baroda, now Vadodara in Gujarat, was an important centre of this patronage under the Gaekwad rulers. Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III supported art and education and acquired works by Indian and European artists.

Sayajirao Gaekwad III and Raja Ravi Varma

Raja Ravi Varma was born in Kerala, but his artistic career had an important connection with the Baroda court. Sayajirao Gaekwad III commissioned paintings from him, including royal portraits and scenes from Indian epics.

The Gaekwad patronage was particularly important during the 1880s. A group of epic paintings was commissioned in 1888. These works connected the court's interest in Indian cultural subjects with Ravi Varma's distinctive realistic style.

The relationship illustrates a central feature of modern Indian art: artists could work across regions. Ravi Varma did not have to be a native of Gujarat to make a major contribution to its artistic heritage. His connection with Gujarat arose through patronage, commissions and the preservation of his works.

The Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum

The Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum in Vadodara preserves an important collection associated with the Gaekwad family. It stands within the Lukshmi Vilas Palace estate, also commonly called the Laxmi Vilas Palace estate.

The collection includes original paintings and portraits by Raja Ravi Varma, alongside Indian and European artworks. Many of these works were collected or commissioned under Sayajirao Gaekwad III.

The museum is housed in the former Motibaug School building and was inaugurated as a museum in April 1961. This date refers to the museum's inauguration, not to the period when Ravi Varma painted for the Gaekwad court.

Ravi Varma's Baroda commissions belong to the late 19th century. The Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum opened in 1961. The collection's history and the museum's inauguration are different events.

Kala Bhavan and the development of education

Sayajirao Gaekwad III also established Kala Bhavan at Baroda in 1890. Its early purpose was primarily technical and vocational education. Training included practical trades such as carpentry, fitting, smithy work and related skills.

The institution demonstrates the ruler's broader interest in education and technical knowledge. However, it should not be confused with Kala Bhavana at Santiniketan, the art-education institution associated with Rabindranath Tagore and Nandalal Bose in Bengal.

Why patronage matters

Patronage did more than finance individual paintings. It helped establish collections, encouraged artistic activity and allowed Indian painters to work for important public figures. At Baroda, royal commissions and art collecting created a lasting connection between a painter from Kerala and the cultural heritage of Gujarat.

Prelims focus

  • Sayajirao Gaekwad III was an important patron of Raja Ravi Varma.
  • The connection was centred on Baroda, now Vadodara in Gujarat.
  • A group of Ravi Varma's epic paintings was commissioned by the Gaekwad ruler in 1888.
  • The Maharaja Fateh Singh Museum is located within the Lukshmi Vilas Palace estate.
  • Kala Bhavan was established at Baroda in 1890.
  • Trap: Baroda's Kala Bhavan is not the same institution as Kala Bhavana at Santiniketan.

[Sources: Queensland Art Gallery and Gallery of Modern Art, collection record for Ram Sagar Darp Haran, account of Sayajirao Gaekwad III's 1888 commission, accessed 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Maharaja Fatesingh Museum Vadodara, museum collection, location and history, accessed 23 November 2026; Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Kalabhavan Workshop, history of the 1890 technical institution, accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: An Indian artist paints at an easel while a court representative examines paintings in a princely art room in 1880s Baroda.
pictures.caption: Royal commissions helped artists produce paintings that later became part of important collections.

pictures.alt: Kala Bhavan in Baroda began technical and vocational education in 1890; Kala Bhavana in Santiniketan is associated with artistic education.
pictures.caption: Two similarly named institutions developed in different places and served different educational purposes.

title: The Gaekwad Rulers of Baroda and Their Contribution to Modern Painting

body:
Why the Bengal School developed

The Bengal School of Art emerged in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with Calcutta, now Kolkata, as an important centre. It became closely associated with the search for an Indian artistic identity during the period of cultural nationalism.

European academic realism had become influential in colonial art schools. Supporters of the Bengal School believed that Indian artists should also study and develop the artistic traditions of their own country. They did not simply reject every new artistic method. Their central aim was to develop an approach in which Indian cultural ideas were expressed through an artistic language informed by Indian traditions.

Abanindranath Tagore and E. B. Havell

Abanindranath Tagore (1871–1951) is regarded as the leading founder of the Bengal School. He encouraged artists to draw inspiration from Indian painting rather than depending entirely on European academic models.

E. B. Havell, a British art educator associated with the Government Art School in Calcutta, supported this effort. From 1896, Havell and Abanindranath worked towards giving Indian artistic traditions a more important place in art education.

Their interest in Indian art was particularly directed towards Mughal and Pahari miniature paintings. These traditions provided examples of distinctive composition, line, colour and storytelling. Bengal School artists also experimented with methods that produced softer and more atmospheric effects than heavily modelled academic oil paintings.

The wash method

One method associated with Bengal School painting was the wash technique. In this approach, diluted colour is applied to produce delicate changes in tone and atmosphere. The result can emphasise mood, suggestion and expression instead of sharply defined, lifelike modelling.

The wash technique was one feature of the Bengal School, not a rule that every artist always followed. The school's significance lay in its wider attempt to develop an Indian approach to modern painting.

Bharat Mata: art and nationalism

Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata in 1905, during the period of the Swadeshi movement and opposition to the Partition of Bengal.

The painting represents the nation symbolically as a female figure with 4 arms. She holds objects associated with basic needs and values: grain, cloth, a book or manuscript, and prayer beads. These represent nourishment, clothing, learning and spiritual life.

The painting illustrates how an artwork could express a national ideal without depicting a political meeting or a battlefield. It connected the idea of the motherland with the welfare and cultural identity of its people.

The original work is associated with the collection of the Victoria Memorial Hall, Kolkata. Its identification with Abanindranath Tagore, rather than Raja Ravi Varma, is an important distinction.

Journey's End

Another important work by Abanindranath Tagore is Journey's End, dated 1913. It shows an exhausted camel at the end of its journey. Its subdued colours and atmospheric treatment demonstrate how the painter could communicate emotion without relying on strongly defined academic realism.

The Bengal School is a modern movement even though its artists drew inspiration from older Indian painting traditions. The use of historical artistic ideas does not make their paintings medieval artworks.

Prelims focus

  • Abanindranath Tagore was the leading founder of the Bengal School.
  • E. B. Havell supported the Indianisation of art education in Calcutta from 1896.
  • Mughal and Pahari miniatures were important sources of inspiration.
  • Bharat Mata was painted by Abanindranath Tagore in 1905.
  • Journey's End by Abanindranath Tagore is dated 1913.
  • Trap: Bharat Mata is not a painting by Raja Ravi Varma.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, An Introduction to Indian Art—Part II, Chapter 6, The Bengal School and Cultural Nationalism, pp. 86–89 and 95–96, reprint 2025–26; Ministry of Culture, National Portal and Digital Repository for Museums of India, Victoria Memorial Hall collection record for Bharat Mata, accessed 23 November 2026.]
